analysis.one_liner: Bans lawsuits blaming food and drink companies for obesity and weight gain.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 306-120 on October 19, 2005, but the Senate never brought it to a vote and it died when that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would bar people from suing food and beverage makers, sellers, advertisers, and their trade associations for injuries tied to weight gain or obesity, and would immediately dismiss any such lawsuits already in court. It would keep only narrow exceptions: cases showing a company knowingly broke an advertising or labeling law that a person relied on, broken express contracts or warranties, and enforcement cases brought by the FTC or FDA [S3] [S4] [S5]. Even in those excepted cases, courts would have to freeze evidence-gathering while dismissal motions were pending and demand detailed written proof of every claim up front [S3] [S4].
analysis.who_benefits: Food and beverage manufacturers, fast-food chains, restaurants, advertisers, distributors, and their trade associations gain the most: they would be shielded from obesity-related lawsuits, including ones already filed, and from the discovery process that can expose internal marketing and labeling documents [S2] [S5].

how_it_helps.text: It prohibits new lawsuits and immediately dismisses pending ones against food makers, sellers, advertisers, and trade associations over weight gain, obesity, or related health conditions [S3] [S5].

It keeps only narrow exceptions: knowing violations of marketing or labeling statutes that a person justifiably relied on, breaches of express contract or warranty unrelated to weight gain, and FTC or FDA enforcement [S3] [S4].

In any case that still fits an exception, the bill freezes discovery during dismissal motions and requires the plaintiff to plead every element, every statute violated, and the specific facts of the exception in advance [S3] [S4].

analysis.who_pays: People injured or sickened in ways connected to what they ate lose their day in court — including people whose lawsuits were already pending and would be thrown out. Consumers generally lose a legal check on how food is marketed, leaving policing to the FTC and FDA alone [S3] [S5].

drawbacks.text: The bill would retroactively dismiss lawsuits already pending in court, taking away a remedy people were actively pursuing when the law changed [S3] [S5].

The exceptions are hard to meet: a plaintiff must show the company knowingly violated a specific statute, intended the person to rely on it, and that this reliance was the direct cause of the injury — a bar that would eliminate most cases [S4].

Supporters argued obesity lawsuits were frivolous and would raise costs for a major industry; critics respond that Congress itself acknowledged obesity has many causes, and if the suits are truly weak, courts can dismiss them without a blanket federal ban that also removes legitimate claims.
By channeling food-marketing oversight exclusively through the FTC and FDA, the bill would leave enforcement to agencies with limited resources, replacing private lawsuits as a backstop.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offers little to ordinary consumers and takes something away: it would wipe out pending lawsuits and block future ones, with narrow exceptions that are difficult to satisfy [S3] [S4]. It does remove the threat of costly litigation that food companies said was unfair, and Congress found that obesity stems from many factors, so blaming a single product is often legally weak [S5]. But the blanket ban applies to all such claims, not just frivolous ones, so the cost falls on consumers with legitimate grievances while the benefit is a liability shield for a large industry.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it by a wide margin, but the Senate let it sit on its calendar and it died when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Ric Keller introduced the bill on February 2, 2005, and it was referred to the House Judiciary Committee [S7].
The Judiciary Committee reported the bill with amendments on June 14, 2005, after a 16-8 committee vote to move it forward [S7].
The House passed the bill 306-120 on October 19, 2005; Republicans supported it nearly unanimously (226-1) while Democrats split 80 for and 118 against [S8].
The Senate received the bill on October 20, 2005, and placed it on its legislative calendar under General Orders, but no further action was ever taken [S7].
The bill never received a Senate vote and died when the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007 [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Consumers and plaintiffs' lawyers came out ahead in the narrow sense that the liability shield never became law, so existing legal remedies against food companies were left intact. The food and beverage industry avoided a new law but also gained nothing beyond the status quo it already had. Its broad House passage shows where the industry's congressional support lay, but the Senate's inaction preserved the legal status quo.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Consumers, whose right to sue was preserved

for.name: Rep. Ric Keller
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Personal Responsibility in Food Consumption Act and steered it through the House.

for.name: House Judiciary Committee
for.what_they_did: Marked up the bill and reported it with amendments by a 16-8 vote on May 25, 2005.

for.name: 80 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Voted yes on final passage alongside nearly all Republicans.

against.name: 118 House Democrats
against.what_they_did: Voted no on final passage, casting nearly all of the 120 votes against the bill.

against.what_they_did: Received the bill and placed it on the calendar but never brought it to a vote before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Republicans backed the bill almost unanimously (226-1), but 80 of 200 voting Democrats joined them, so the 306-120 win was large despite a majority of Democrats voting no [S8].

industries.industry: Food and beverage manufacturers and sellers (including fast-food chains)
industries.note: The bill would give the industry a near-total shield from obesity-related lawsuits, including retroactively dismissing cases already in court. Its gain comes directly from taking away consumers' legal recourse over how food is made and marketed [S3] [S5].

Advertisers and marketers are named protected parties, so the bill would remove the main legal threat over how food products are promoted to consumers, with only knowing statutory violations still actionable [S3].

The bill would eliminate the business of obesity-related lawsuits against food companies and add pleading hurdles to what remains. Its loss corresponds to consumers losing access to representation for these claims [S2] [S3].
